nutshell: Humans frequently 'see faces' in random stimuli like coffee stains or clouds (pareidolia), but computer vision face detectors trained only on human faces largely miss this. The paper releases 'Faces in Things', a 5,000-image human-annotated pareidolic face dataset, shows that fine-tuning a face detector on animal faces (not pareidolic data at all) closes roughly half the gap to full pareidolic fine-tuning, and proposes two simple statistical models that both predict a 'peak pareidolia' effect at moderate image complexity - confirmed in both a human psychophysics study and the fine-tuned detectors. Not a person-ReID paper - a face-detection/perception paper pulled in by this corpus's broader search terms.
contributions: Faces in Things: a 5,000-image dataset of web-sourced pareidolic faces (via CLIP retrieval over LAION-5B), manually annotated with bounding boxes plus attributes (perceived emotion, gender, intentionality, difficulty), with real human/animal faces filtered out; split 70/30 train/test.

Empirical finding that a SOTA face detector (RetinaFace) trained only on human faces barely detects pareidolic faces (7.9%/2.8% AP for MobileNet/ResNet50 backbones), but fine-tuning on animal faces alone - despite containing no pareidolic images - roughly doubles that AP (16.7%/15.4%), closing about half the gap to fine-tuning on pareidolic data directly (33.9%/27.1%); the effect is reciprocal (pareidolic fine-tuning also improves animal-face detection), suggesting a shared generalist face-detection representation.

Two independent simple statistical models of pareidolia - a Gaussian spectral-mode model and a Poisson spatial-feature model - that both predict a 'peak pareidolia' effect: face-like perception is maximized at a moderate level of image complexity, and drops off when images are too simple or too detailed.

Empirical confirmation of the predicted peak-pareidolia effect in both a human psychophysics experiment (subjects viewing noise images of varying spatial-frequency complexity) and the fine-tuned face detectors evaluated on the same stimuli - both show the same inverted-U response curve.
deficiencies: The dataset's own attribute breakdown (Fig. 3) shows 53% of the 5,000 images are labeled 'Design' rather than 'Accident' - i.e., deliberately face-like objects (product designs, printed smileys, etc.) rather than spontaneous pareidolia like coffee stains or clouds, which is the phenomenon the paper's framing and Hamlet epigraph emphasize. This means roughly half the dataset may not be testing the intended 'accidental' perceptual phenomenon.

The dataset's annotations (bounding boxes and all facial attributes) come from what the acknowledgments describe as essentially one primary annotator ('hundreds of hours of annotations' by a single named person) with no inter-annotator agreement or reliability statistics reported, despite attribute claims like '31% of faces are considered challenging to spot' being used as descriptive findings.

Table 1's AP numbers (the paper's central quantitative result) are reported as single point estimates with no confidence intervals or repeated-run variance, in contrast to the human psychophysics results (Fig. 11) which do report a 95% confidence interval - the machine-side headline numbers get a lower evidentiary bar than the human-side ones in the same paper.

The claimed match between human and machine 'peak pareidolia' (Fig. 11) is described as showing 'the same characteristic pareidolic peak,' but the peak occurs at a Gaussian filter width of ~16 for humans versus visibly closer to ~4 for the machine models - a roughly 4x difference in exactly where the peak sits that the text doesn't quantify or reconcile, even though matching peak location (not just peak existence) would be the more rigorous version of the claim.
notable: The Animal+Pareidolia t-SNE visualization (Fig. 7) shows RetinaNet's internal features for animal and pareidolic faces clustering together and separately from human faces - the authors note this quantitatively via clustering but also flag, almost as an aside, that some points resemble a frog, i.e., the model may be latching onto genuinely animal-like visual structure in 'random' pareidolic images rather than a generic face-like signal. Also notable given this literature review spans many non-face-detection papers: the dataset explicitly excludes real human and animal faces by construction, so all reported gains are attributable to a shared low/mid-level visual feature space rather than any leakage of real faces into the pareidolic set.
